title: Sales & Business Development
tagline: Find buyers, earn trust, and close — the complete path from first cold call to enterprise deals.
summary: Sales is the revenue engine of every company and one of the few careers where results, not credentials, drive advancement. This roadmap covers the full craft: prospecting and qualification, discovery and demos, negotiation and closing, account growth, pipeline math, and the methodologies (SPIN, MEDDIC, Challenger) modern teams use.

sources.label: BLS OOH — Wholesale and Manufacturing Sales Representatives

detail.description: Sales matches a buyer's problem to a solution and guides the decision to purchase. Underneath the vocabulary, it is a repeatable process: find people with the problem, understand it deeply, show a credible fix, and make the decision easy.
detail.why: Sales roles exist in every industry, hire continuously, and reward skill faster than almost any other function. It is also superb training for running any business.
learn: Read the BLS profile of sales representatives for the career shape
Identify the stages of a standard B2B sale
Follow 5 sellers on LinkedIn for a month and note how they communicate
Write down 3 problems you have personally 'sold' someone on

resources.title: BLS OOH — Wholesale and Manufacturing Sales Representatives

tasks: Sell goods or services to businesses or individuals; explain product features and negotiate prices and terms.

detail.description: B2C sales are short, emotional, and high-volume; B2B sales are long, multi-stakeholder, and rational on the surface. Deal size, cycle length, and the number of decision-makers differ sharply.
detail.why: The two games need different temperaments and skills. Knowing which you prefer shapes everything: role choice, company size, and even the methodologies worth learning.
learn: Compare a $30 consumer purchase with a $30,000 software purchase: cycle, stakeholders, risk
Identify the buying committee roles in B2B: champion, economic buyer, users, blockers
Explain why B2B deals stall and who un-stalls them
Pick your preference and shortlist companies that match

detail.description: A defined sales process stages every deal — prospecting, qualification, discovery, proposal, negotiation, close, handoff — so forecasts mean something and coaching is possible.
detail.why: Companies hire against their process. Speaking its language fluently (stages, exit criteria, definitions) makes you productive from week one.
learn: Diagram a 6-stage B2B sales process with exit criteria per stage
Define what makes a deal 'qualified' at each stage
Map where deals commonly die and why
Compare how a startup and an enterprise define the same stages

detail.description: Customer relationship management systems (Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive) track every contact, activity, and deal. Pipeline hygiene — accurate stages, next steps, and dates — is table stakes.
detail.why: Your pipeline is your credibility: managers coach from it and forecasts depend on it. Sloppy CRM data is the most common rookie failure.
learn: Understand core objects: leads, contacts, accounts, deals, activities
Log 10 mock activities with correct associations
Move deals through stages with honest probabilities
Pull one pipeline report and explain what it says

detail.description: The ideal customer profile defines which organizations buy most and stay longest (size, industry, triggers); personas describe the humans inside them (role, goals, fears).
detail.why: Random outreach fails; targeted outreach works. ICP thinking is the difference between noise and relevance, and it drives every downstream tactic.
learn: Write an ICP for a product you know: firmographics, triggers, disqualifiers
Draft 2 personas: role, day-in-the-life, pain, objections
List 20 companies matching your ICP
Justify each disqualifier with a cost-of-serving argument

detail.description: Prospecting creates conversations: cold calls, cold email, warm referrals, and event follow-ups — in sequences with personalized opening lines and a single clear ask.
detail.why: Prospecting is the #1 skill of entry-level sales (the SDR job) and the hardest to automate well. People who can start conversations are never unemployed.
learn: Write a 4-touch sequence: email, call, email, breakup
Draft cold emails under 90 words with one ask
Practice a 20-second cold call opener and objection pivot
Track reply and connect rates; iterate weekly
tasks: Contact new and existing customers to persuade them to purchase goods or services.

detail.description: Social selling builds visibility and trust where buyers already are — mainly LinkedIn: a credible profile, useful commentary, and patient relationship-building before any ask.
detail.why: Modern buyers research you before replying. A strong presence warms every cold touch and compounds over a career.
learn: Rewrite your LinkedIn headline and About section for your buyer
Comment usefully on 10 industry posts per week for a month
Publish 4 short posts teaching something real
Convert 1 warm conversation into a discovery call

detail.description: Discovery is diagnostic: understanding the buyer's current state, desired future state, cost of inaction, and decision process — before any pitch. Good discovery sounds like consulting, not selling.
detail.why: Deals are won or lost in discovery. The best reps talk for perhaps a third of the call and still control it completely.
learn: Prepare a 12-question discovery framework (situation, problem, impact, decision)
Practice summarizing what you heard before responding
Quantify one prospect's problem in money or time
Role-play a discovery call and count your talk ratio

resources.title: O*NET — Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing

detail.description: Frameworks structure qualification: BANT (budget, authority, need, timeline), MEDDIC (metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identify pain, champion), and lighter variants.
detail.why: Time is a seller's only inventory. Qualification discipline protects it, and framework vocabulary is expected in interviews at most B2B companies.
learn: Explain BANT and when its simplicity wins
Map MEDDIC letters to questions you would ask
Score 5 mock deals for qualification and forecast them
Know when to walk away — write your own disqualification rules

detail.description: Active listening — full attention, confirmation summaries, layered follow-ups — plus open and diagnostic questioning are the raw mechanics of discovery.
detail.why: Buyers trust people who understand them. Listening is also trainable and immediately separates you from most sellers, who pitch too early.
learn: Practice paraphrase-and-confirm on every conversation for a week
Convert 10 closed questions into open ones
Use the 3-deep follow-up: why does that matter?
Record (with permission) one call and self-score your listening

detail.description: A value proposition connects your solution to the buyer's quantified problem: what changes, by how much, over what time — expressed in the buyer's numbers, not your features.
detail.why: Deals clear procurement when value is explicit. Feature lists stall; business cases move.
learn: Rewrite a feature list as a business-outcome story
Build a simple ROI calculator for a product you know
Practice the 'so that…' chain until you reach money
Tailor one value story to two different personas

detail.description: A great demo is a story about the buyer's day made better — not a feature tour. Structure: their problem, the moment of value, proof, and a clear next step.
detail.why: Demos are the emotional peak of B2B deals. Sloppy demos un-do great discovery; sharp ones make champions out of attendees.
learn: Design a 10-minute demo following problem → value moment → proof
Cut a feature tour down to the 3 moments your persona cares about
Handle 'can it also…?' detours gracefully
Rehearse on video and cut your intro to 60 seconds

detail.description: Objections ('too expensive', 'we're fine as-is', 'need to think') are requests for more information or confidence. The craft: acknowledge, clarify the real concern, respond with evidence, confirm resolution.
detail.why: Most deals die from unhandled objections, and most reps argue instead of exploring. Calm objection handling is a career-long differentiator.
learn: List the 8 most common objections in your market
Practice acknowledge → clarify → respond → confirm on each
Distinguish objections from conditions (real blockers)
Write proof points (case studies, data) for your top 3

detail.description: Negotiation trades value instead of discounting blindly: know your walk-away, concede slowly and conditionally, and keep a list of non-price trades (term length, start date, scope, references).
detail.why: Discount discipline protects both your commission and the company's economics. Skilled negotiators close better deals with happier buyers.
learn: Define your walk-away and opening positions for a sample deal
Practice conditional concessions: 'If you…, then we…'
List 6 non-price variables you can trade
Debrief one negotiation: what would you trade differently?

detail.description: Closing turns agreement into a signed contract: timeline alignment, paper process management, signature logistics — then a clean handoff to onboarding so the value promise survives.
detail.why: Deals restart endlessly without paper-process management, and sloppy handoffs cause early churn that reflects on you at renewal.
learn: Ask for the business naturally: define mutual next steps with dates
Map a paper process: legal review, procurement, signatures
Write a handoff document a customer success team would praise
Set post-sale expectations with the buyer before signing

detail.description: Post-sale selling — renewals, upsells, cross-sells, QBRs (quarterly business reviews) — is where long-term sellers earn most: expansion revenue is cheaper and stickier than new logos.
detail.why: Account management and customer success are major hiring pipelines, and expansion skills make you valuable in almost any sales org.
learn: Build a 90-day post-sale check-in cadence
Run a mock QBR: value delivered, goals ahead, expansion idea
Spot 5 expansion signals (usage growth, new stakeholders, budget cycles)
Map one account's whitespace honestly

detail.description: Formal buying processes need written artifacts: proposals structured around the buyer's outcomes, and RFP responses assembled with legal, security, and product teams on deadline.
detail.why: Common in enterprise, government, and vendor management — strong proposal skills open door to higher-velocity deal types.
learn: Outline a 5-section proposal: problem, impact, solution, proof, terms
Answer 10 standard RFP questions crisply
Learn to say 'no' to unpaid custom work politely
Build a reusable asset library for repeat questions

detail.description: Pipeline management keeps a portfolio of opportunities honest: coverage ratios against quota, stage discipline, next-step dates, and regular scrubs that kill dead deals.
detail.why: Your pipeline is your income. Sellers who manage coverage proactively hit quota; those who hope, don't.
learn: Compute your required pipeline coverage (commonly 3–4× quota)
Run a weekly self-scrub: kill, advance, or date every deal
Maintain next steps on 100% of open deals for a month
Balance new, progressing, and closing deals by week

detail.description: Forecasting predicts what will actually close this period: weighted pipeline, commit vs best-case categories, and honest calls that leaders can run the business on.
detail.why: Forecast accuracy is the fastest trust-builder with sales leadership and the core skill of the manager interview loop.
learn: Explain commit / best case / pipeline categories
Apply stage-weighting to a sample pipeline
Call a month-end number and reconcile it after
Identify your personal sandbagging or happy-ears bias

detail.description: The dashboard of selling: activity volume, connect and reply rates, meetings held, conversion by stage, average deal size, sales cycle length, win rate, and quota attainment.
detail.why: Metrics make improvement possible. Knowing your own conversion rates tells you exactly what to fix and how much activity to add.
learn: Compute your funnel math: activities → meetings → opps → wins
Find your weakest stage conversion and design one fix
Explain average deal size and cycle length trade-offs
Build a one-page personal scorecard and review it weekly

detail.description: Methodologies codify how to sell: SPIN Selling's situation-problem-implication-need questions, Challenger's teach-tailor-take-control, MEDDIC's qualification rigor, Sandler's pain funnels.
detail.why: Teams run on one methodology; interviews test whether you know it. Understanding several makes you adaptable — and a better interviewer of employers.
learn: Summarize SPIN, Challenger, and MEDDIC in one line each
Match each methodology to deal type it suits best
Read a primary source (e.g., SPIN Selling) and extract 5 practices
Blend two methodologies into your own discovery framework

detail.description: Stories carry proof: customer-before/customer-after narratives, specific numbers, and named outcomes beat adjectives. The best sellers speak in cases, not claims.
detail.why: Proof lowers buyer risk — the real obstacle in most deals. A library of stories lets you answer objections before they're voiced.
learn: Write 5 customer stories in the before/after/result format
Attach a number to every story you tell
Practice the 90-second version and the 15-second version
Collect 3 'objection-matched' stories per common objection

detail.description: Sales is a rejection-heavy profession. Sustainable performers manage energy and ego deliberately: activity routines, loss reviews without self-flagellation, and separating self-worth from win rate.
detail.why: Most people who leave sales leave because of unmanaged rejection. Building the psychological toolkit early keeps you in the game long enough to get good.
learn: Design a daily activity block you can hold for 90 days
Write a 5-minute loss-review template: what did I control?
Build a support network of peers outside your company
Practice reframing 'no' as data — track what you learned

detail.description: Ethical selling means selling only what genuinely fits, representing products honestly, respecting no, and never pressuring vulnerable buyers. Long-term trust out-earns short-term tricks.
detail.why: Reputation compounds in sales like nowhere else — references and repeat buyers are the entire senior career. Ethical lapses end careers and appear in every negotiation you'll ever have.
learn: Learn your industry's regulatory constraints (e.g., financial services suitability rules)
Practice disqualifying a bad-fit buyer out loud
Understand consent, privacy, and anti-spam basics for outreach (CAN-SPAM/GDPR concepts)
Write your personal 'lines I won't cross' list

detail.description: The standard B2B ladder: SDR/BDR (outbound prospecting) → account executive (closing) → senior/enterprise AE → team lead → sales manager → director/VP/CRO. Adjacent tracks: customer success, partnerships, revenue operations.
detail.why: Sales promotions are performance-gated, not tenure-gated. Understanding the ladder lets you pick companies where your target rung is reachable.
learn: Map typical tenure and metrics per rung in your market
Decide new-logo vs expansion vs channel track
Identify 3 target companies with a real SDR→AE path
Draft the specific quota attainment you need to earn promotion

detail.description: Sales has few universal licenses; credentials are mostly vendor training — HubSpot's free Inbound Sales and Sales Software certifications being the most cited. Product companies run their own intensive onboarding academies.
detail.why: Certifications signal coachability to hiring managers, but a documented outreach experiment or mock discovery tape beats them. Do both cheaply.
learn: Complete HubSpot's free Inbound Sales certification
Complete the Sales Software (CRM) certification
Record a 10-minute mock discovery call as a portfolio artifact
Note: most 'sales certifications' are internal programs — ask interviewers about theirs

certs.name: HubSpot Inbound Sales Certification
certs.note: Free course and exam on the inbound selling methodology; commonly listed on entry-level sales resumes.

detail.description: Selling differs by context: SMB velocity vs enterprise rigor, inside vs field sales, channel/partner sales, technical and manufacturing sales (where domain knowledge dominates), and regulated industries with compliance constraints.
detail.why: Choosing your vertical early compounds domain expertise — the strongest moat a seller can build.
learn: Compare SMB, mid-market, and enterprise selling on cycle and stakeholders
Explore technical/industrial sales where O*NET's wholesale reps dominate
Learn one regulated vertical's basic rules (e.g., medical devices, financial products)
Pick a vertical and read its trade publication for a month

detail.description: Sales pay is typically base + commission against a quota, with accelerators above target and clawbacks on churned deals. OTE (on-target earnings) splits vary by role and risk level.
detail.why: Evaluating offers requires understanding quota-to-OTE math, ramp expectations, and territory quality — not just the headline OTE.
learn: Learn the vocabulary: OTE, quota, accelerator, draw, clawback
Model two offers: 50/50 vs 70/30 base/commission splits
Ask the right interview questions: attainment distribution, ramp time, territory
Understand why >100% of reps missing quota matters to you

resources.title: BLS OOH — Wholesale and Manufacturing Sales Representatives

detail.description: Sales leadership (manager → director → VP) trades personal selling for hiring, coaching, forecasting, and territory design. The best managers coach process, not personality.
detail.why: Leadership is one of two senior paths (the other: enterprise/strategic accounts). Knowing what the job actually is — coaching math and people — helps you decide early.
learn: Shadow a sales manager for a day if possible
Learn 1:1 coaching structures (pipeline review, call review)
Study how territories and quotas are designed
Decide: player-coach track vs senior IC track — both pay well
